speaker: teacher

detail: The teacher apologises for the name and says he could not come up with a better one. Four topics in total: Gravatar, on-demand image optimization, tagging photos, newly unread message indicator.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: a very interesting high level pattern that you can use or that a lot of company uses in production to prevent major outages

statement: Designing a notification system for Instagram was covered only once, in the teacher's first cohort (March, about two years back), and is on YouTube as his first-ever video (sort by oldest); students should watch it rather than have it repeated.
detail: Teacher says the video shows how naive he was when explaining it, yet people found it amazing, which shows the massive gap that exists; everything else in it the class can now design on its own, but watch it for the fan-out bit.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I covered this one system just once, designing notification for Instagram on my first ever

statement: Kafka's parallelism is limited by its number of partitions.
detail: Recalled from yesterday's discussion.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the parallelism of Kafka is limited partitions in Kafka

statement: Fan-out example: when Justin Bieber posts something, a notification must go to his 10-15 million (or however many) followers, i.e. notifications to millions of users.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Let's say Justin Bieber posted something.

statement: For such massive fan-out, using Kafka alone is pathetically slow when you have a limited number of partitions, and adding a large number of partitions becomes a problem.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Because if you use Kafka, it's pathetically slow.

statement: High-level pattern for very high fan-out: club a message stream (Kafka or Kinesis) with a message broker (SQS or RabbitMQ).
detail: This is how notification systems are built at scale; the key takeaway of the teacher's notification-system video is why this decision is made.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: where you club Kafka with SQS. So message stream with message broker to get very high degree of fan-out.

statement: Simply drawing a single message broker that broadcasts the message is not what happens at scale; that is not how you handle scale.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: No, that's not what happens at scale.

statement: The teacher had to send notifications to about 50,000-60,000 users within five seconds for aggressive marketing; they did it by stitching a message stream with a message broker to get high-degree fan-out.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I'm just talking about few 50, 60,000, but in the span of five seconds, we had to do it.

statement: Before designing Gravatar, the class looks at how images are actually served; understanding this helps build a huge number of features, and companies use it in impressive ways.
detail: A practical demo follows.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: let's spend a bit of time to understand how images are served.
flags: check: sentence cut off, words possibly lost

statement: Saying "images are served" hides the work: someone has written the code that reads the image and serves it, so the real question is how a static file is served.
detail: When asked, people answer without thinking about it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Someone has to read image and serve it.
flags: unclear: "will you see it into service?"

statement: A browser does not know a URL is an image URL from its extension (e.g. .jpg); the browser has no clue.
detail: Some people thought this four or five weeks back.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: No, browser does not have a clue.

statement: A browser is a dumb piece of software with a fixed, defined behaviour for everything; the same applies to apps.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Browser is a dumb, stupid piece of software.

statement: Platforms (the browser, the Android OS, iOS, their SDKs) are building blocks, so they cannot be very smart; they must stay basic enough to be used with hundreds of other things.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: they're all platform, they're all building block, so they cannot be very smart

statement: To render an image you put its URL in an IMG tag's SRC; while rendering the HTML, the browser hits the IMG tag and makes an HTTP GET request to whatever URL is in SRC.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: whatever you provide in IMG SRC tag, it makes an HTTP GET request.

statement: The browser has no idea what the GET will return; it expects an image and tries to interpret whatever comes back in the response as an image.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Whatever you get in the response, it tries to interpret it as an image.

statement: Every file format has a header that identifies it: the PNG header says the file is PNG; JPG, bitmap and TIFF have headers too.
detail: Recalled from yesterday's demo of uploading an image on GitHub issues, where the PNG bytes with the PNG header and some RDF data were sent.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: The header of the PNG file tells you that it's a PNG file.

statement: On a 2xx response the browser checks the header of the returned bytes, decides the format (e.g. PNG), invokes the matching decoder and renders the decoded image as pixels.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: if it's a 2xx response, whatever bytes you to get in the response, it checks the header.

statement: Every browser ships with image decoders (mostly decoders, not really encoders) for every format: PNG, JPG, TIFF, SVG and others.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: every browser ships with image encoders and decoders, but rather mostly decoders, not really encoders

statement: The GET request for an image URL (e.g. on arpitbhayani.me) reaches the web server, which looks up the handler for that path.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It's a web server. What it would do is it would see what's the handler of this path.

statement: A static folder mapping maps a URL path like /static to a folder on local disk; you configure it in nginx, Spring Boot, Flask, Django - every framework supports a static folder path.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Every framework supports a static folder path.

statement: With /static mapped, whatever follows /static in the URL is treated as a relative file path; the server reads that file from the static folder and sends its bytes as the response, without caring whether it is an image, text or anything else.
detail: Restated at 00:12:04: the backend code reads the URL, extracts the path after /static, goes to that relative path in the static directory, reads the content in bytes and sends it back.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: interpret whatever is there after slash static as a relative file path, go to my static folder on the disk

statement: Example: /static/img/appy.jpg - the server finds that path in the mapped static folder, reads the file's bytes and returns them; the browser renders them as an image because the URL was in an IMG tag.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So for example, slash static slash IMG slash appy.jpg.

statement: Static file serving is not automatic: it is a piece of code written into the web server so you do not have to re-implement it again and again.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: There's a piece of code written in your web server so that you don't have to re-implement it again and again.

statement: Instead of relying on /static, you can write your own handler that reads the file from somewhere else, for example from S3 instead of local disk.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I can write my own handler that instead of reading file from local disk, it reads file from S3.

statement: Example handler: expose /raw/<path>; whatever path follows /raw is used as the S3 key in a configured bucket, the file is read and returned (e.g. http://localhost:5000/raw/...).
detail: Very similar to /static, which reads the same relative path from local disk; here it is read from S3.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we're literally using that as a key of S3 present in this bucket, reading the file and sending it to the user.

statement: With one generic URL (no per-file configuration on S3) and three or four lines of code, the /raw handler is a proxy for S3.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So with this three, four lines of code, what we just built is we built a proxy for S3.

statement: The /raw handler is not a feature or a new CDN; it only shows the possibility of returning images as part of a normal HTTP response, before seeing practical applications.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I'm not designing a new CDN.

statement: Many people think a web server can only send JSON responses; it can do a lot more, including sending images from HTTP handlers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: A lot of people for some reason think that we can only send JSON responses from Web server.

statement: Because the handler is in your control, the image need not already exist: the handler can run custom logic, and all that matters is the bytes sent; if they are a properly structured, byte-serialized image, the browser renders it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it is not really needed that your image already exists for it to read and serve.

statement: Sharing a GitHub repository link (the teacher's DiceDB project) on Twitter, LinkedIn or Facebook renders a social snippet with the title, site name, description and an image.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It rendered a social snippet of it.

statement: The snippet image is specific to the repository (DiceDB/dice): description and number of contributors, issues, discussions, stars and forks; GitHub generates it on the fly (not on every request).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This image is generated on the fly by GitHub, not every time, but on the fly by GitHub.

statement: The snippet image comes from the Open Graph protocol (OG): the HTML you serve specifies og:image, and the URL given there is rendered as the image in the snippet.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This is part of Open Graph protocol called OG.

statement: In GitHub's page source the og:image content is a URL that returns the same image when opened, yet its path does not end in .jpg, .png or any image extension.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If you look carefully, it does not end with .jpg, .png, anything like that.

statement: The og:image URL returns a valid image as a byte response, but that does not mean GitHub stored the image on S3.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But now this does not mean that this image is stored on S3 somewhere by GitHub.

statement: The data in the image reflects the repository's current state (e.g. contributor and fork counts); if it changes, the image changes too, maybe after a day or two, so it is very recent and not pre-generated.
detail: Example: if a student becomes a DiceDB contributor, the contributor count would change.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Maybe it would take one day or two days to reflect, but it's very recent.

statement: Many people think such images are pre-generated; they are not. With millions of repositories, GitHub would not spend compute generating one per repository every day; the image is generated on demand when requested.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: A lot of people think everything is pre-generated. No, it is not.

statement: GitHub's og:image URL is essentially the same kind of route handler as the /raw/<path> handler, put behind a CDN; placed in an IMG tag it renders without any hiccup.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: this is literally the route handler that we wrote

statement: GitHub hosts a separate CDN for Open Graph images, opengraph.githubassets.com, alongside the githubusercontent.com CDN for user assets, similar to edge.arpitbhayani.me seen yesterday.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This is another CDN that it has opengraph.githubassets.com.

statement: Flow: the backend sends the image URL (whose key stays constant for a repository, or can be generated on the fly) to the frontend; the frontend puts it in an IMG tag; the request goes to the CDN, which serves the image if it has it cached, without going to the backend server every time.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This request goes to CDN hosted at opengraph.githubassets.com.

statement: On a CDN miss, the CDN calls the origin, which is GitHub's API server; it handles the request by generating the image on the fly.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Origin is the API server of GitHub, which handles this request, which is generating this image on the fly.

statement: The image is a template: every repository gets the exact same format, with the title, repository icon and fetched key statistics placed in fixed positions.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This is a template, no matter which image you, which repository you pick, you would see this exact same format.
flags: check: phrase unclear, very fast segment

statement: Images are generated on the fly with libraries such as ImageMagick or PIL; there are tons of such libraries.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: there is a library called PIL, there is a library called ImageMagick around tons of libraries out there to generate images on the fly.

statement: The API server responds to the CDN with the generated image; the CDN caches it with some TTL and serves subsequent requests; after expiry (e.g. a day) the next request is a CDN miss, goes to the backend and a new image is generated on demand.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: CDN caches the file. And then with some TTL, it keeps it there and serves it to the user.

statement: GitHub does not create and store this image for every repository; it cannot pre-generate them because the image contains recent information, so it generates them on demand.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: because the image itself contains the recent information, which is why GitHub cannot pre-generate those images and store it.

statement: On-demand generated social images appear in hundreds of places; Bannerbear is a company specializing in this, and it makes social sharing easy, interactive and real time.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Bannerbear, always specializing in doing this.

statement: Hypothetical: Twitter could natively generate a nicely formatted OG image of a tweet when its URL is shared (instead of LinkedIn influencers screenshotting tweets with poet.so); on a CDN miss Twitter's API server would fill a template with the tweet, format it, respond, and the CDN would cache it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If Twitter tomorrow wants to do this

statement: Dynamic social images are very powerful for user experience: the user sees personalized, very recent information (current likes, shares, comments, reposts) right in the shared image rather than a static representation.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: user sees personalized things, user sees something which is very recent.

statement: Build a local prototype of on-the-fly social images (hardly one hour of work): install Python, pick an image library, expose an API endpoint that fetches a GitHub repo's information, creates the image on the fly and serves it via localhost.
detail: Java or any other language also has such libraries; the teacher used Python. Same thing works for any GitHub repo in the world. You learn a lot from doing it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: And you can literally build this in hardly one hour.

statement: PIL (Python Image Library) is typically the best library for generating images; it internally uses ImageMagick through a C++ binding and gives a native Python interface.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It internally uses ImageMagick. It has a C++ binding to that.

statement: Earlier, sharing a GitHub link rendered a big, poor-looking avatar of the user, a poor experience; GitHub implemented generated repository images to make sharing repositories on social media pleasant.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Earlier, if you remember, when you shared images, GitHub used to render a very pathetic avatar of that user.

statement: Nothing taught is theoretical: everything discussed in the course is used in production by some company and can be prototyped on your local machine; you do not need 50,000 servers.
detail: Nothing beats practical experience.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: There is no such thing that I need 50,000 servers to do that.

statement: Gravatar creates a single embeddable URL for your profile picture, which is why some websites can show your picture even though you did not sign up with Twitter, Gmail, Microsoft or similar.
detail: With the image-serving context built, Gravatar becomes an easy problem.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So what Gravatar does is it creates your single embeddable URL for your profile picture.

statement: On gravatar.com you log in with your email, upload a bunch of profile pictures and mark one of them as active.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I can upload a bunch of profile pictures there. I can mark one of them as active.

statement: The Gravatar URL is gravatar.com/<MD5 hash of the email>; it is constant because passing the same value to a hash function always gives the same output.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It's an MD5 hash of my email ID.

statement: The Gravatar URL (e.g. https://gravatar.com/0eafd172) put in an IMG SRC returns the current profile photo as image bytes; it does not redirect to some page.
detail: Similar to the S3-reading handler seen earlier.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This is actually returning the image as bytes over here.
flags: unclear: "reading from a message and survey data"

statement: If every platform adopted Gravatar, it would hash your email and render your photo anywhere from that one URL; changing your photo means uploading it on gravatar.com and marking it active, and the next request picks it up everywhere without any social network doing anything.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Everywhere your profile photo is changed without any social network have to do anything.

statement: Platforms obviously do not all adopt Gravatar, but it is a very novel concept.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But they don't obviously do that. But it's a very novel concept.

statement: A system like Gravatar can be prototyped in three or four hours; scaling it is the difficult part, building a prototype is not, so build as many prototypes as you can.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So that's why I recommend build prototypes as many as you can

statement: Gravatar requirements: a user can upload multiple pictures; a user can mark one of them as active; when the API is requested, the active one is returned in the response.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: first, user can upload multiple pictures on Gravatar; second, user can mark one of them as active

statement: Brainstorming the Gravatar design starts with the database: which tables, what schema, what to store.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Let's start with database.

statement: Student proposal: the users table stores the hash of the user's email ID.
detail: The teacher first has the hash crossed off as derivable (00:34:02), then adds it back as an indexed column for query performance (00:42:24).
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: With the user table where user gives his email ID and we store the hash for it.

statement: Student proposal: store only the hash and not the actual email, since one is derivable from the other, it saves space, and unlike social platforms Gravatar does not need to display the email.
detail: Teacher corrected: you do want to see your email on your Gravatar profile page; you need it to authenticate people / let them log in; and with a hash collision someone would be logged into another person's account.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: you might need to display that email ID somewhere, but at Gravatar we don't need to display.

statement: It is always better to store the actual email ID: users log in and are authenticated with it, it is shown on the profile page, and relying on the hash risks a collision logging someone into another person's account.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It's always better to store email ID.

statement: Initial users table: id and email; the hash is deliberately not stored (written and crossed off) because it is a derivable attribute.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You're not, you're deliberately not storing hash because it is derivable.

statement: A single column of a relational database cannot hold multiple image paths, so a user's multiple photos go in a separate photos table.
detail: A student wondered whether image paths should go in the users table or a different table.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: How would you store multiple paths in a single column of relational DB?

statement: Photos table: id (primary key) and user_id; there is one row per uploaded photo, so a user with 10 photos has 10 rows, and all of them must be rendered.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So all the photos uploaded by the user will go over here. Right? ID, user ID.

statement: Student proposal: store the paths of the images in the photos table.
detail: Teacher corrected: recall yesterday's discussion - the path can be derived, so it need not be stored.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Do we really need to do that? Recall yesterday's discussion. Can you not derive it?

statement: The photos table also gets an is_active column (boolean, true/false) marking the user's active photo.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So let's call it is active.

statement: Query for all photos of a user (to render them on the UI): select * from photos where user_id = ?; no is_active filter is needed because all photos are shown and only one is active.
detail: A student suggested filtering on is_active; the teacher said all are shown.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: No, no, we'll show all of them because only one of them is active, right?

statement: The request carries the hash of the email, not the user ID, so the photos query must join photos with users (photos.user_id = users.id) and filter on the user found by that hash.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Because what you are getting over here is a hash of email ID.

statement: Student proposal: reverse or decrypt the incoming hash to get the email ID.
detail: Teacher corrected: you cannot get the email from the hash - it is hashing, not encryption; hashing is lossy, so the actual email cannot be recovered.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: You cannot get email from the hash. It's not encryption. It's hashing.

statement: Without a stored hash, the query can apply the hash function in the where clause: where HASH(email) = <the provided hash>.
detail: This works functionally; the teacher then asks what is wrong with it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But can you not just do pass the hash function where hash of email is equal to the one that you provided?

statement: Hash collisions between two users' emails are accepted in this design: assume hashes are unique, since two people with the same hash could not be disambiguated anyway.
detail: Raised by a student as the problem with the HASH(email) query; the teacher set it aside.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Assume that hashes are unique.

statement: Student observation: the HASH(email) query adds computation on every query (a hash of email each time), so it is not a simple query even if hashing is lightweight.
detail: The teacher pushes further by asking how many rows the query would scan (10,000 rows example).
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: You are doing hash of email every time. Each query you are adding this computation.

statement: Student answer, praised by the teacher as the pain point: because of the hash in the where clause the database must read every row, compute each email's hash and compare it, a whole-table scan, before it can do the join.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Because of this hash. Yeah, for each email ID, we have to create that hashing and evaluate that.

statement: A computation in the where clause (e.g. HASH(email) = ?) prevents the database from using indexes: it has no way to know which email evaluates to that hash without computing it for every row, so every query is a full table scan.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the where clause itself contains a computation, which means that it cannot leverage indexes over here

statement: Fix: store a hash column in users, index it and query where users.hash = ?; the lookup becomes very pointy (almost O(1)) - filter the one user row, get the user ID and join to photos - very quick.
detail: This query is very common, so without the column it would be very expensive.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This is why you need hash column over here, because then you can index it

statement: It is not always true that you should not store what is derivable: it depends - if not storing it slows things down, store the redundant value.
detail: The teacher explicitly contradicts yesterday's principle that whatever is derivable should not be stored.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So it's not always true that what is derivable, you should not store it, depends

statement: When a user is created, store the email and also compute and store the hash of the email; email is a unique key and hash is a unique key, both indexed.
detail: Teacher phrases it as creating an index on literally every single column.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Email is a unique key, hash is a unique key.

statement: Drawing boxes is easy; the devil lies in the details - only by writing the query and figuring out how it executes do you discover that a column you thought unnecessary is needed for performance.
detail: The hash column is the classic example; scratching the surface shows the ugliness of the system.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Unless you write that query, unless you figure out how that would execute

statement: Student query to mark a photo active: update photos set is_active = true where id = <photo id>.
detail: The student first wanted to pass user ID too; the teacher said it is not required because id is the primary key.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Update photos. Set is active equal to true where user ID equal to.

statement: Student proposal: also passing user ID in the update would make the scan smaller on the table.
detail: Teacher corrected: id is the primary key, so the lookup is anyway log n and already very efficient.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: No, ID is primary key, scan would anyway be log n. So that's very efficient anyways.

statement: The three-line mark-active update is one of the simplest queries you could write (almost hello world), yet it has a big problem that almost every engineer has seen and should never make.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Three line query, one of the most simplest query that you could write, almost hello world.

statement: Problem 1 (from a student): the update does not mark the previously active photo as inactive.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: So you don't mark the previously active image as inactive.

statement: Student fix: run two queries - first mark all of the user's photos as inactive (update photos set is_active = false where user_id = ?), then mark the chosen one as active.
detail: The student's naive first idea was three queries (fetch the active one, mark it inactive, mark the new one active), and a counter-based hack was abandoned; the teacher asked to simplify, and it became two.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Actually you can do two queries. You can just mark all as false and then mark one as true.

statement: Student refinement: instead of marking every photo false, add "and is_active = true" to the first update's where clause so it only touches the currently active row.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Just add "and" in the where clause and say is active is true.

statement: Student answer: the second update depends on the first and should only run once the first completes, so the two updates can be made a transaction.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: or we can make it as a transaction, something like that.

statement: The two updates must explicitly be wrapped in a transaction: if the process crashes after the first update, the user is left with no active photo, and e.g. Facebook rendering the profile photo gets a 404 not found.
detail: Teacher's words: "every photo is marked as active and you don't have any active photo" - the intended meaning appears to be marked inactive.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So this needs to explicitly be wrapped in a transaction.
flags: check: teacher says "every photo is marked as active" while describing no active photo

statement: Wrapping in a transaction sounds obvious but people skip it and do not call it out explicitly; focus on every intricate detail, especially in simple systems, because what seems obvious is not.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Very simple thing, but people skip it.

statement: Student point: with the transaction the update is atomic, so concurrent requests are taken care of.
detail: Teacher accepted ("concurrency taken care of") and asked what else could go wrong, hinting at the second query.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Once we have added transaction, it becomes atomic in nature, right?

statement: Problem 2: the second update (set is_active = true where id = ?) must also check user_id = ? so a user can only change his or her own photos.
detail: Another student first suggested the missing user ID; the teacher challenged it (photo id is the primary key, why pass user ID?) until a student gave the ownership reason, which the teacher called brilliant.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Yeah, I think user ID is required because a user should be allowed to change only his or her photos, not everyone.

statement: Without the user_id check, someone could pass a random photo ID from the frontend: the first update marks your own photos inactive while the second marks someone else's photo active, leaving you with no active photo; the check is for security and correctness of the system.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Imagine someone from the front end passing a very random photo ID.

statement: A really simple use case has many hidden intricacies; going into such implementation details - why a field is needed, ensuring correctness in all possible cases - is what makes you a better engineer.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: how a very simple use case, really simple use case, has so many hidden intricacies.

statement: With the updates wrapped in a transaction (plus the ownership check) and the redundant hash column stored, the Gravatar system is both efficient and correct.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we are ensuring our system is efficient and correct.

statement: It is exactly like code reviews: write five lines of code and get 50 comments, write 500 lines and get "looks good to me"; with a simple system people nitpick every single thing.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: When you write five lines of code, you'll get 50 comments. When you write 500 lines of code, you'll get looks good to me.

statement: Query run when the Gravatar URL is hit, to pick the user's active photo: select * from photos join users on photos.user_id = users.id where users.hash = ? and photos.is_active = true; it returns one photo because correctness ensures only one is active.
detail: A student first added a filter on photos.id; the teacher corrected it to photos.is_active.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: No, no, no, not photos ID but photos dot is active. Photos dot is active true.

statement: There is one very minor optimization possible in the active-photo query; it is extreme nitpicking and in practical use cases the performance difference is very minimal.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: In practical use cases you might see very minimal performance difference, very minimal

statement: Using an inner join instead of a left join is not the optimization: here an inner join performs exactly the same.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Inner join would work exactly the same performance as left left in that.

statement: The most frequent query on Gravatar is getting the active photo and rendering it; with active_photo_id in users it avoids the join and becomes select * from users where (hash) = ?, which yields the active photo ID and user ID, from which you create the S3 path, read the file and serve it.
detail: The teacher stresses this is extreme nitpicking: avoiding this very small join is not a massive performance difference.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: The most frequent query on your platform would be this, right?

statement: A student asked why is_active is needed in the photos table at all; the teacher: it was there to mark one of multiple photos active, and with active_photo_id in users, the rare query "is this photo active?" can be answered by joining with users.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: Why do we need to store is active in the photos table?

statement: Two designs: is_active in the photos table versus active_photo_id in the users table; with the latter the most frequent query needs no join - it is literally a primary key lookup.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Either you store it as active in the photos table or you store active photo ID in the users table

statement: With active_photo_id, marking a photo active no longer requires marking others inactive: it is a single update query (with the two user checks), and with auto commit a single query is a transaction in itself, so no multi-query transaction is needed.
detail: Reading becomes a plain select * from users where id = ?; you get the user ID and photo ID, build the S3 path, read the image and serve it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If you have auto commit, a single query is a transaction in itself.

statement: Putting active_photo_id in users is counterintuitive because we think is_active is a property of the photo, not the user: in class design, low-level design and schema design we tend to think in terms of attributes of an entity, which is why most people put is_active in photos.
detail: Thinking a little out of the box, the design is oversimplified.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But it is very counterintuitive because you think is active is a property of photo, not a user.

statement: There is no one way to build a system: what seems simple is not when you go into the details, and many things can be challenged.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: There is no one way to build the system, right?

statement: In every cohort since the teacher started asking this question (this is the 15th cohort), people start with is_active in photos because we are trained to think that way, which might not be optimal; the class was walked through it as a natural progression rather than jumping to the answer.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: every single cohort, people start with is active over here because we are trained to do so.

statement: The teacher does not claim active_photo_id is hugely more optimal; the point is that a somewhat more optimized solution can exist, so always challenge your own beliefs: unlearn, relearn and become better.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So always be handy in challenging your own beliefs, unlearn, relearn and become a better, right?
